name: Braille tactile writing for words and music
description: A tactile writing system organized around a six-dot cell, enabling blind readers to read and write text and music.

impact.note: Gave blind readers independent reading and writing across many societies, a small share of humanity; later codes and devices are direct successors.

date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: Louis Braille published his method of dot-based writing for words and music.
events.population: Students and teachers at the Paris institution for blind youth

evidence.supports: LOC reprint dates the publication of Braille’s writing and music system to 1829.

events.caveats: Early music notation included some dashes and was refined later; the six-dot cell did not appear in modern form overnight.

evidence.supports: LOC reprint dates the publication of Braille’s writing and music system to 1829.

date.label: during Braille’s lifetime, by 1852
date.basis: Source describes use during Braille’s lifetime; 1852 is his death, not a date of first use.

events.statement: A Library of Congress biography reports that students learned the method themselves during Braille’s lifetime because it was not officially taught.
events.caveats: Bounded by Braille’s death in 1852; does not imply no teacher used or taught the system.

evidence.supports: The biography describes informal access during his lifetime.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest dated witness established by the cited source for this scoped record, not a claim of global first.

caveats: Raised print letters and Barbier’s night writing predated Braille. Published and institutional-acceptance dates should not be conflated.

research.note: Initial sourced research; independent review pending. Independent reader checked Library of Congress publication, early music notation and informal student access, bounded only by death.
